newsitem.title: INDONESIA: FEATURE - Indonesia finds colonial past in urban jungle.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Indonesia finds colonial past in urban jungle.

text.p: Tucked between the Java Sea to the north and the skycrapers of Jakarta's "golden triangle" business district to the south is a slice of Indonesia's colonial past almost untouched by booming development.

Dating from the 17th Century when it was the hub of the Dutch East India Company's colonial trading empire, the Kota area of Indonesia's capital has for years been passed over by property developers focussing on the fast-growing business district.
The government wants that to change, says Wisnu Murti, an official at Jakarta's Building Renovation Bureau.
"We want to turn Kota into a heritage area... Indonesians' awareness should be developed so there is more and more appreciation of this old part of town," Wisnu told Reuters in an interview.
The aim is to recapture some of Kota's old colonial charm and attract tourists who have tended to stay clear of overcrowded Jakarta and flock instead to the country's beach resorts, Wisnu said.
The once whitewashed colonial townhouses which are now grey with pollution will be restored to their former glory.
The network of canals built by the Dutch will be dredged of debris left by years of neglect.
One problem, however, was funding, Wisnu said. The government hopes the lion's share of costs will be borne by the private sector.
"The idea of developing the waterfront area has attracted many developers and people with money," Wisnu said, but declined to elaborate.
At the moment, however, there are only a handful of real estate projects aimed at refurbishing Kota.
Analysts said that interesting investors who already make huge profits in the Central Business District (CBD) is not going to be easy.
Jakarta-based architect Michael Sumarijanto said current Asian development thinking does not allow room for the idea of heritage.
"This region (Asia) is maybe experiencing the age of the machine... profit becomes the dominant value replacing the arts, culture and education," Sumarijanto said.
Developers can make huge sums building mega office blocks and see no profit incentive in rebuilding a dilapidated remnant of Jakarta's past, he said.
"There are many things to be done to make this area favourable to investors," said Bayou Utomo, a property consultant with Jakarta-based Procon Indah.
"It depends on the commitment of the government... to develop the existing infrastructure. Currently traffic jams are terrible in Kota."
A company owned by President Suharto's daughter Siti Hardianti Rukmana plans to build a subway which will open up Kota to the southern city, but work is not planned to start until 2003.
Another problem is that linking up investors and owners of the old Dutch buildings has been problematic, Bayou said.

"The investment scheme will be more complicated (than in the CBD) because we don't know who owns the land. It has not been proven yet whether this kind of venture can be succesful in that area," he said.
With most funds diverted to other areas of the city, the dream of regaining Kota's former elegance is going to take time, Wisnu admitted, ruefully.
"It will not be finished for 20 years or so," he said.
